column2: What is the core difference between Amazon SQS and Amazon SNS?
column3: SQS stores messages in a queue for consumers to poll and process; SNS pushes each publication to subscribed endpoints.
column4:
SQS supports decoupled work queues, while SNS supports publish/subscribe fan-out.
Example: An order is placed in SQS for one worker to process, while an SNS topic sends the order notification to email, Lambda, and another queue.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_1_—_Cloud_Foundations_&_IaC type::comparison topic::Messaging topic::Decoupling

column2: An order-processing service must absorb traffic spikes and let workers process jobs independently. Which service is the best fit?
column3: Amazon SQS. It buffers each job in a queue until a worker is ready to process it.
column4:
A queue buffers work and decouples producers from consumers so each side can scale independently.
Example: An online store places each order in a queue, and available workers process the orders at their own pace.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_1_—_Cloud_Foundations_&_IaC type::scenario topic::Messaging topic::Asynchronous_processing

column2: One alarm must notify email recipients, a Lambda function, and an SQS queue at the same time. Which service fits?
column3: Amazon SNS. It publishes one message to multiple subscribed destinations.
column4:
An SNS topic can fan one publication out to multiple subscribed endpoints.
Example: One CloudWatch alarm publishes to an SNS topic whose subscribers include an email address, a Lambda function, and an SQS queue.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::scenario topic::Messaging topic::Fan-out

column2: What does Amazon EC2 provide?
column3: Resizable virtual compute instances in AWS.
column4:
EC2 gives customers control of the guest operating system and application stack on virtual machines.
Example: A team launches a Linux EC2 instance, selects its CPU and memory size, and installs its own web application.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_1_—_Cloud_Foundations_&_IaC type::recall topic::Compute topic::Virtual_machines

column2: A team needs MySQL but wants AWS to manage the underlying database infrastructure and routine platform operations. Which service should it evaluate?
column3: Amazon RDS. It runs familiar relational database engines while AWS handles much of the infrastructure work.
column4:
RDS is a managed relational database service; the customer still owns data, access, schemas, and configuration choices.
Example: A company runs PostgreSQL on RDS so AWS handles backups and database infrastructure while the team manages its schema and data.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_1_—_Cloud_Foundations_&_IaC type::scenario topic::Databases topic::Managed_services

column2: What does Infrastructure as a Service provide, and what major control remains with the customer?
column3: It provides virtualized infrastructure; the customer retains control of the guest operating system, applications, data, and many configurations.
column4:
IaaS removes physical-hardware ownership without removing workload administration.
Example: AWS supplies the EC2 hardware and virtualization, while the customer patches the guest OS and manages the application.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_1_—_Cloud_Foundations_&_IaC type::recall topic::Service_models topic::IaaS

column2: How are the AWS Management Console, CLI, SDKs, and IaC tools related to AWS service APIs?
column3: They are different interfaces that ultimately invoke AWS service APIs.
column4:
“Single unified API” is only a mental model; it is not the name of one AWS product or one literal endpoint.
Example: Creating a bucket through the console or CLI ultimately results in a request to the S3 service API.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_1_—_Cloud_Foundations_&_IaC type::recall topic::APIs topic::Cloud_management

column2: What benefits does Infrastructure as Code provide?
column3: Repeatable, version-controlled, reviewable, and automated infrastructure provisioning.
column4:
Machine-readable definitions reduce manual configuration drift and support consistent environments.
Example: A version-controlled template creates the same network in development and production instead of relying on manual clicks.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_1_—_Cloud_Foundations_&_IaC type::recall topic::Infrastructure_as_Code topic::Automation

column2: Why is Terraform better described as an orchestrator than as an application compiler?
column3: It builds a plan and calls provider APIs to reach a desired infrastructure state; it does not produce an application binary.
column4:
Terraform reads HCL and coordinates resource changes through provider APIs.
Example: Terraform compares configuration with current infrastructure, creates a plan, and calls provider APIs; it never compiles the web application itself.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_1_—_Cloud_Foundations_&_IaC type::comparison topic::Infrastructure_as_Code topic::Terraform

column2: Complete the relationship: An AWS Region contains multiple isolated ________.
column3: Availability Zones.
column4:
Regions are separate geographic areas, and multi-AZ design provides isolation within a Region.
Example: A workload runs in two AZs in the same Region so one data-center failure does not stop the service.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::cloze topic::Global_infrastructure topic::Regions

column2: What is an Availability Zone?
column3: One or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking, and connectivity within an AWS Region.
column4:
AZs are designed for fault isolation while maintaining low-latency connectivity to other AZs in the Region.
Example: A workload runs in two AZs in the same Region so one data-center failure does not stop the service.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::recall topic::Global_infrastructure topic::Availability_Zones

column2: What is the geographic scope of an Amazon VPC?
column3: A VPC belongs to one AWS Region and can span that Region’s Availability Zones.
column4:
Subnets divide the VPC at the AZ level.
Example: A VPC in eu-west-1 can contain subnets in several AZs there, but it cannot extend into eu-central-1.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::recall topic::Networking topic::VPC_scope

column2: Can one subnet span multiple Availability Zones?
column3: No. A subnet resides entirely within one Availability Zone.
column4:
An Availability Zone can contain multiple subnets, but a subnet cannot cross AZ boundaries.
Example: A company creates one public and one private subnet in each of two Availability Zones for resilience.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::recall topic::Networking topic::Subnets

column2: An EC2 instance is placed in a subnet whose route table has a route to an internet gateway. Is the instance automatically reachable from the internet?
column3: No. It also needs an appropriate public address and security rules that allow the traffic.
column4:
A route makes the subnet public, but internet reachability depends on routing, addressing, and filtering together.
Example: A public web server needs a public IP, a route to the internet gateway, and security rules allowing HTTPS.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::scenario topic::Networking topic::Public_subnets

column2: Why might `us-east-1a` refer to different physical zones in two AWS accounts?
column3: Availability Zone letter mappings can differ by account.
column4:
Use AZ IDs when different accounts must coordinate on the same physical Availability Zone.
Example: Two accounts compare the AZ ID use1-az2 because the label us-east-1a may map differently in each account.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::recall topic::Global_infrastructure topic::Availability_Zone_IDs

column2: How can an S3 bucket be Regional while its name is globally unique?
column3: The bucket’s data resides in a selected Region, while its name must be unique across the general-purpose bucket namespace.
column4:
A global console view and global naming do not mean that bucket data is automatically stored worldwide.
Example: The name company-receipts must be globally unique, but its objects can still reside only in the selected eu-west-1 Region.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::comparison topic::Storage topic::Global_infrastructure

column2: Which THREE factors commonly influence AWS Region selection?
column3: Latency to users, regulatory or data-location requirements, and service availability or price.
column4:
Region choice is a business and technical decision; no single Region is best for every workload.
Example: A company chooses Frankfurt because its users are nearby, required services are available, and data must remain in the EU.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::multiple-response topic::Global_infrastructure topic::Region_selection

column2: Which two practices best protect the AWS account root user?
column3: Enable MFA and reserve the root user for tasks that explicitly require it.
column4:
The root user has unrestricted account access and should not be used for routine administration.
Example: An administrator uses a normal role every day and opens the root account only for a task that specifically requires root.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::scenario topic::Root_user topic::MFA

column2: Does an IAM user require its own external email address or payment method?
column3: No. It is an identity defined inside one AWS account.
column4:
Usage performed by the IAM user is billed to the AWS account.
Example: A developer can have an IAM identity inside the company account without owning a separate AWS account, email subscription, or payment method.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::recall topic::IAM_users topic::Identities

column2: Distinguish authentication from authorization.
column3: Authentication verifies who the caller is; authorization determines what that identity may do.
column4:
Both are required to securely evaluate AWS requests.
Example: Signing in proves Alice’s identity; her policies then decide whether she may read a particular S3 bucket.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::comparison topic::Authentication topic::Authorization

column2: What permissions does a newly created IAM identity receive merely by existing?
column3: None. Permissions must be granted through applicable authorization policies and mechanisms.
column4:
AWS access is not granted automatically to a new identity.
Example: A newly created analyst user cannot open an S3 report until an applicable policy explicitly grants read access.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::recall topic::IAM_policies topic::Default_permissions

column2: Complete the common IAM policy elements: Effect, Action, Resource, and optional ________.
column3: Condition.
column4:
Conditions narrow when a statement applies, such as by source, time, tags, or other context keys.
Example: A policy permits an administrative action only when the request is authenticated with MFA.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::cloze topic::IAM_policies topic::JSON

column2: A developer needs read access to one S3 bucket for one project. Which approach follows least privilege?
column3: Grant only the required read actions on that bucket, not broad administrator or all-S3 permissions.
column4:
Least privilege limits permissions to the task and resource actually required.
Example: A reporting user receives only read access to one reports bucket, not administrator access to the account.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::scenario topic::Least_privilege topic::IAM_policies

column2: What are the two parts of an IAM access key?
column3: An access key ID and a secret access key.
column4:
Both are used to sign programmatic requests; the secret access key is retrievable only when created.
Example: A CLI profile may contain AKIA… as the access key ID and a separate secret value used together to sign requests.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::recall topic::Access_keys topic::Programmatic_access

column2: How can an IAM user rotate an access key without an abrupt application outage?
column3: Create the second key, update and test the application, then deactivate and delete the old key.
column4:
An IAM user can have at most two access keys, which supports an overlap during rotation.
Example: Create a second key, switch and test the application with it, and only then deactivate and remove the first key.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::scenario topic::Access_keys topic::Rotation

column2: What is the preferred alternative to long-lived access keys for AWS workloads?
column3: IAM roles and temporary security credentials.
column4:
Temporary credentials reduce the risk and maintenance burden of static secrets.
Example: An EC2 application assumes a role and receives temporary credentials instead of storing a secret key in a file.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::recall topic::Temporary_credentials topic::IAM_roles

column2: Who patches the guest operating system on an Amazon EC2 instance?
column3: The customer.
column4:
AWS secures the physical infrastructure and virtualization layer; the customer manages the guest OS and applications.
Example: For EC2, AWS maintains the physical host, but the customer installs operating-system security updates.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::scenario topic::Shared_responsibility topic::EC2

column2: Which Lambda security responsibilities remain with the customer?
column3: Function code and libraries, data, IAM permissions, and resource configuration.
column4:
AWS manages the underlying infrastructure, operating system, and managed runtime platform.
Example: AWS patches Lambda infrastructure, while the customer fixes a vulnerable library bundled with the function.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::scenario topic::Shared_responsibility topic::Serverless

column2: Do service control policies grant permissions?
column3: No. SCPs set the maximum available permissions for principals in member accounts.
column4:
IAM or resource policies must still grant access, and an explicit restriction from an applicable SCP limits the result.
Example: An SCP blocks member accounts from disabling CloudTrail, but an IAM role still needs its own permission to use CloudTrail.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::recall topic::Organizations topic::Service_control_policies

column2: A company needs to record resource configurations and evaluate them continuously against rules. Which service fits?
column3: AWS Config. It records resource configuration history and evaluates resources against compliance rules.
column4:
AWS Config records supported configuration history and evaluates compliance. Remediation is optional and must be configured.
Example: Config shows that a security group became noncompliant after someone opened port 22 to the whole internet.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::scenario topic::Compliance topic::Configuration_auditing

column2: Distinguish data residency from data sovereignty.
column3: Residency is where data is physically stored; sovereignty is the legal jurisdiction and authority governing it.
column4:
Compliance requirements may impose controls based on both location and jurisdiction.
Example: Customer records may physically reside in Germany, while applicable law determines which government has legal authority over them.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::comparison topic::Compliance topic::Data_governance

column2: Which AWS environment is designed for eligible U.S. government and highly regulated workloads with isolated Regions?
column3: AWS GovCloud (US).
column4:
GovCloud has specific eligibility and access requirements; it is not simply a general Region available to any individual.
Example: An eligible U.S. government contractor runs a regulated workload in an isolated AWS GovCloud (US) Region.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::scenario topic::Compliance topic::Government_workloads

column2: List the defining characteristics of a security group.
column3: It is stateful, applies at the resource network-interface level, and supports allow rules only.
column4:
Security groups evaluate all applicable rules and automatically allow response traffic for an allowed flow.
Example: A web server security group permits inbound HTTPS, and the response traffic is allowed automatically.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::recall topic::Network_security topic::Security_groups

column2: List the defining characteristics of a network ACL.
column3: It is stateless, applies at subnet boundaries, supports allow and deny rules, and processes numbered rules in ascending order.
column4:
Inbound and outbound traffic are evaluated separately.
Example: A subnet NACL denies a known malicious CIDR and separately permits the required inbound and outbound traffic.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::recall topic::Network_security topic::Network_ACLs

column2: When should a security group be preferred over a network ACL?
column3: Use security groups for fine-grained resource access; use NACLs as coarse-grained subnet guardrails or defense in depth.
column4:
Security groups are more versatile because they are stateful and can reference other security groups.
Example: Use a security group to allow HTTPS to selected servers; add a NACL when the whole subnet needs a coarse rule such as denying one CIDR.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::comparison topic::Network_security

column2: A security group allows an inbound HTTPS request. Must a separate outbound rule allow the response to that request?
column3: No. Response traffic is automatically allowed because security groups are stateful.
column4:
State tracking permits the return flow regardless of outbound rules.
Example: A web server security group permits inbound HTTPS, and the response traffic is allowed automatically.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::scenario topic::Network_security topic::Stateful_firewalls

column2: Which VPC control can explicitly deny a known malicious IP range for an entire subnet?
column3: A network ACL. It can apply an explicit deny rule to traffic crossing the subnet boundary.
column4:
NACLs support deny rules at subnet boundaries; security groups support allow rules only.
Example: A subnet NACL denies a known malicious CIDR and separately permits the required inbound and outbound traffic.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::scenario topic::Network_security topic::Explicit_deny

column2: Is an S3 bucket placed inside a customer VPC subnet?
column3: No. S3 is a managed Regional service outside customer subnets.
column4:
VPC resources can reach S3 through public service endpoints or supported VPC endpoints.
Example: An S3 bucket is not launched into 10.0.1.0/24; private VPC resources reach the Regional S3 service through an endpoint.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::recall topic::Storage topic::VPC_architecture

column2: Which services support gateway VPC endpoints, and what is the endpoint charge?
column3: Amazon S3 and DynamoDB; there is no additional charge for the gateway endpoint.
column4:
Gateway endpoints add service-prefix routes to selected VPC route tables.
Example: A route table can send private S3 or DynamoDB traffic through a free gateway endpoint instead of a NAT gateway.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::recall topic::VPC_endpoints topic::Gateway_endpoints

column2: How does an interface VPC endpoint connect a VPC privately to a service?
column3: It creates elastic network interfaces with private IP addresses and uses AWS PrivateLink.
column4:
Interface endpoints can use security groups and normally incur endpoint-hour and data-processing charges.
Example: A private application reaches Secrets Manager through private endpoint IP addresses protected by a security group.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::recall topic::VPC_endpoints topic::Interface_endpoints

column2: EC2 instances in a private subnet need ordinary same-Region access to S3 without a NAT gateway and without an endpoint-hour charge. What should be used?
column3: An S3 gateway VPC endpoint. It provides private S3 access through route-table entries without an hourly endpoint charge.
column4:
A gateway endpoint routes S3 traffic through selected route tables with no additional endpoint charge.
Example: Private instances reach S3 through a route-table entry without using a NAT gateway.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::scenario topic::VPC_endpoints topic::Service_selection

column2: A company needs a dedicated, predictable network connection from its data center to AWS. Which service fits?
column3: AWS Direct Connect.
column4:
Direct Connect establishes dedicated connectivity for hybrid bandwidth and consistency requirements.
Example: A data center uses a dedicated link to AWS for more consistent hybrid network performance than an internet-based connection.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::scenario topic::Hybrid_networking

column2: Which service caches HTTP/HTTPS content at edge locations close to viewers?
column3: Amazon CloudFront. It caches web content near viewers to reduce latency and origin load.
column4:
CloudFront is AWS’s content delivery network and reduces origin load and viewer latency.
Example: A website caches images at edge locations so distant visitors do not fetch every image from the origin Region.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::scenario topic::Content_delivery topic::Caching

column2: What does a CloudFront invalidation do?
column3: It removes selected objects from CloudFront caches before their normal expiration.
column4:
Use invalidation when updated content must be fetched from the origin before its TTL expires.
Example: After correcting a CSS file, a team invalidates that path so viewers receive the new version before the old TTL expires.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::recall topic::Content_delivery topic::Caching

column2: What does AWS Global Accelerator provide for an IPv4 accelerator by default?
column3: Two static anycast IPv4 addresses that route supported traffic through the AWS global network.
column4:
Global Accelerator improves network-path performance and failover without caching application content.
Example: A global game uses two fixed anycast IP addresses to route UDP players onto the AWS network without caching content.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::recall topic::Network_acceleration topic::Anycast

column2: When should CloudFront be selected instead of Global Accelerator?
column3: Choose CloudFront when HTTP/HTTPS content should be cached; choose Global Accelerator for network acceleration and static anycast entry points without caching.
column4:
Both use edge infrastructure, but they solve different layers of the problem.
Example: CloudFront caches website images near viewers; Global Accelerator instead speeds a non-cacheable game connection through static anycast IPs.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::comparison topic::Content_delivery topic::Network_acceleration

column2: Globally distributed users must upload large files to one distant S3 bucket faster. Which feature should be evaluated?
column3: S3 Transfer Acceleration. It uses AWS edge locations and optimized network paths to speed long-distance S3 transfers.
column4:
It uses AWS edge infrastructure and optimized network paths for long-distance S3 transfers.
Example: Users in several continents upload large video files to one distant S3 bucket through nearby AWS edge locations.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::scenario topic::Data_transfer topic::Edge_networking

column2: Distinguish AWS Local Zones from AWS Wavelength.
column3: Local Zones place selected AWS infrastructure near metro areas; Wavelength places infrastructure within communications-provider networks for carrier-edge workloads.
column4:
Both reduce latency, but the target access environment differs.
Example: A metro rendering workload may use a Local Zone, while a 5G vehicle application may use a Wavelength Zone inside a carrier network.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::comparison topic::Edge_computing

column2: A workload needs AWS-managed infrastructure installed at the customer’s premises for local processing. Which service fits?
column3: AWS Outposts. It brings AWS-managed infrastructure and selected services into the customer’s own facility.
column4:
Outposts extends AWS infrastructure, APIs, and selected services to customer locations.
Example: A factory processes data locally on AWS-managed racks installed in its own building because it needs very low on-premises latency.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::scenario topic::Hybrid_cloud topic::On-premises

column2: What storage model does Amazon S3 provide?
column3: Regional object storage accessed through APIs.
column4:
S3 stores objects in buckets; prefixes create a folder-like view but not a traditional mounted file system.
Example: A photo is stored as an object in a bucket and retrieved through an S3 API request rather than mounted as a disk block.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::recall topic::Storage topic::Object_storage

column2: What storage model does Amazon EBS provide?
column3: Durable block storage volumes for Amazon EC2.
column4:
An EBS volume behaves like a block device and must be in the same AZ as the attached instance.
Example: A database server attaches an EBS volume as a block device in the same Availability Zone.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::recall topic::Storage topic::Block_storage

column2: Is it always true that one EBS volume can attach to only one EC2 instance?
column3: No. That is the normal model, but supported io1/io2 volumes can use Multi-Attach with multiple Nitro-based instances in the same AZ.
column4:
Multi-Attach is constrained and requires applications or clustered file systems that safely coordinate writes.
Example: Two supported Nitro instances in one AZ attach the same io2 volume, while a cluster-aware application coordinates their writes.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::Storage topic::Multi-Attach

column2: What storage model and protocol does Amazon EFS provide?
column3: Elastic shared file storage using NFS.
column4:
Multiple compute instances can mount the same EFS file system. EFS does not provide SMB.
Example: Hundreds of Linux EC2 instances mount the same EFS directory over NFS.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::recall topic::Storage topic::File_storage

column2: Match S3, EBS, and EFS to their primary access models.
column3: S3 = object/API; EBS = EC2 block device; EFS = shared NFS file system.
column4:
Choose storage by access semantics, sharing, and workload needs.
Example: Store photos as S3 objects, attach EBS as one server’s disk, and mount EFS when many Linux servers need the same directory.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::comparison topic::Storage topic::Service_selection

column2: Does an EBS volume always survive termination of its EC2 instance?
column3: Not always. EBS can persist independently, but a delete-on-termination setting may remove it.
column4:
Persistence capability and lifecycle configuration are different facts.
Example: A root EBS volume marked delete-on-termination disappears with the instance, while a retained data volume can survive.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::Storage topic::Persistence

column2: What persistent storage does a standard AWS CloudShell environment provide?
column3: A 1 GB home directory per supported Region, retained until 120 days of inactivity in that Region.
column4:
Temporary storage outside the home directory is recycled; CloudShell VPC environments do not have the same persistent home storage.
Example: A script saved in the CloudShell home directory remains available when the user returns to that Region later.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::recall topic::Developer_tools topic::Persistent_storage

column2: What are the main functions of Amazon CloudWatch?
column3: Collect metrics and logs, visualize dashboards, and create alarms and automated responses.
column4:
CloudWatch focuses on operational telemetry and application/resource health.
Example: A CloudWatch alarm sends a notification when an application’s error metric exceeds its threshold.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::recall topic::Monitoring topic::Observability

column2: An administrator wants EC2 guest-memory utilization in CloudWatch. Is it available as a standard EC2 metric?
column3: No. Install the CloudWatch agent or publish a custom metric.
column4:
The EC2 service exposes infrastructure metrics such as CPU, but guest OS memory requires in-instance telemetry.
Example: The CloudWatch agent running inside an EC2 instance publishes memory utilization that EC2 does not provide by default.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::scenario topic::Monitoring topic::EC2_metrics

column2: Does creating an AWS Budget automatically impose a hard spending cap?
column3: No. Budgets monitor thresholds and notify; optional budget actions must be configured separately.
column4:
Resources keep running by default after a budget threshold is crossed.
Example: Crossing an $500 Budget threshold sends an alert, but the running EC2 instances continue unless a separate budget action is configured.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::recall topic::Cost_management topic::Budgets

column2: When should AWS Budgets be used instead of AWS Cost Explorer?
column3: Use Budgets for thresholds, alerts, and optional actions; use Cost Explorer to analyze and visualize cost and usage trends.
column4:
One watches against a target; the other supports investigation and analysis.
Example: Use Cost Explorer to discover last month’s increase, then create an AWS Budget to alert when next month’s forecast reaches $500.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::comparison topic::Cost_management

column2: Distinguish CloudWatch from AWS Budgets.
column3: CloudWatch monitors operational telemetry; AWS Budgets tracks cost or usage against financial or consumption thresholds.
column4:
Both can alert, but they observe different data and answer different questions.
Example: CloudWatch alarms when application latency rises; AWS Budgets alerts when forecasted monthly spending crosses a financial threshold.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::comparison topic::Monitoring topic::Cost_management

column2: A short-term, irregular EC2 workload cannot be interrupted and has no predictable long-term baseline. Which pricing model fits?
column3: On-Demand Instances. They require no long-term commitment and are billed for the capacity used.
column4:
On-Demand requires no long-term commitment and suits irregular non-interruptible use.
Example: A temporary test server runs for two days with no commitment and is then terminated.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::EC2_pricing topic::On-Demand

column2: A fault-tolerant batch workload can handle interruption and should minimize EC2 cost. Which capacity fits?
column3: EC2 Spot Instances. They use discounted spare capacity but must tolerate possible interruption.
column4:
Spot uses spare capacity at a large discount but can be interrupted.
Example: A rendering job saves checkpoints so it can resume elsewhere if AWS interrupts its discounted Spot instance.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::EC2_pricing topic::Spot

column2: What commitment is exchanged for Savings Plans discounts?
column3: A consistent amount of eligible compute usage, measured in dollars per hour, for one or three years.
column4:
Savings Plans are more flexible than EC2 Reserved Instances across eligible compute usage.
Example: A company commits to a predictable hourly amount of compute usage for one year to receive lower prices.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::recall topic::Pricing_models topic::Savings_Plans

column2: Are EC2 Reserved Instances separate physical servers?
column3: No. They are a billing discount applied to matching On-Demand usage; some zonal RIs also provide a capacity-reservation benefit.
column4:
The term describes a pricing benefit, not a special instance object running by itself.
Example: A running matching EC2 instance receives an RI billing discount; purchasing the RI did not create or dedicate that server.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::recall topic::Pricing_models topic::Reserved_Instances

column2: How does a container differ from a virtual machine?
column3: A container shares a host OS kernel, while a virtual machine includes a guest OS on virtualized hardware.
column4:
Containers are typically lighter and start faster; VMs provide a separate guest OS boundary.
Example: Several containers share one host kernel, while each virtual machine boots and maintains its own guest operating system.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::comparison topic::Compute_models topic::Containers

column2: Is a cluster itself an orchestrator?
column3: No. A cluster is a logical grouping or capacity boundary; ECS or EKS provides orchestration.
column4:
Scaling capacity and distributing traffic are handled by services such as Auto Scaling and Elastic Load Balancing, not by the word “cluster” itself.
Example: A group of EC2 capacity forms a cluster, but ECS or Kubernetes decides where the containers should run.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::recall topic::Containers topic::Clusters

column2: Distinguish ECS, EKS, and Fargate.
column3: ECS is AWS container orchestration, EKS is managed Kubernetes, and Fargate provides serverless compute capacity for supported ECS or EKS workloads.
column4:
Fargate is a compute option, not a third competing orchestrator.
Example: Use ECS for AWS-native orchestration, EKS for Kubernetes compatibility, and Fargate with either when you do not want to manage worker servers.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::comparison topic::Containers topic::Serverless

column2: Which AWS service stores private container images for later deployment?
column3: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). It securely stores container images that ECS or EKS can later deploy.
column4:
ECR is a managed container image registry integrated with AWS container services.
Example: A CI pipeline pushes version 2.0 of an image to ECR, and an ECS service later pulls that image for deployment.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::Containers topic::Registries

column2: Developers want to upload web application code while AWS provisions load balancing, scaling, and health monitoring. Which service fits?
column3: AWS Elastic Beanstalk. It deploys application code while managing resources such as compute, scaling, and load balancing.
column4:
Beanstalk orchestrates underlying AWS resources while the team retains visibility and control of them.
Example: Developers upload a web application, and Beanstalk creates and monitors the EC2, scaling, and load-balancing environment.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::Application_deployment topic::Managed_platforms

column2: A small business wants a simple bundled VPS with predictable monthly pricing for a basic website. Which service fits?
column3: Amazon Lightsail. It combines common cloud resources into a simplified bundle with predictable pricing.
column4:
Lightsail packages simplified compute, storage, networking, and plans for straightforward workloads.
Example: A small company launches a basic website using a bundle that includes a virtual server, storage, and transfer allowance.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::Compute topic::Simple_hosting

column2: When should Lightsail be chosen instead of Elastic Beanstalk?
column3: Choose Lightsail for a simple bundled VPS and predictable plan; choose Beanstalk for code-centric deployment on scalable standard AWS resources.
column4:
Both simplify deployment, but their abstraction and scaling models differ.
Example: A basic company website may use a fixed Lightsail bundle; a web application needing configurable autoscaling and load balancing may use Beanstalk.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::comparison topic::Application_deployment

column2: Which service schedules batch jobs and provisions supported compute environments to run them?
column3: AWS Batch. It schedules batch jobs and provisions the supported compute capacity needed to run them.
column4:
AWS Batch is designed for queued batch workloads and can use Spot capacity when interruptions are acceptable.
Example: A nightly scientific workload submits thousands of jobs, and AWS Batch schedules them onto suitable compute capacity.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::Batch_computing

column2: A company wants utilization-based rightsizing recommendations without automatically changing resources. Which service fits?
column3: AWS Compute Optimizer. It analyzes utilization and recommends better-sized resources without changing them automatically.
column4:
Compute Optimizer analyzes metrics and configurations to produce recommendations; the customer decides whether to apply them.
Example: Compute Optimizer notices a lightly used EC2 instance and recommends a smaller type; the owner decides whether to change it.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::Cost_optimization topic::Rightsizing

column2: What is the AWS Nitro System’s role in modern EC2?
column3: It uses dedicated hardware and a lightweight hypervisor architecture to offload and isolate many networking, storage, management, and security functions.
column4:
Nitro reduces virtualization overhead and enables capabilities such as EC2 bare metal integration.
Example: Nitro hardware offloads networking and storage tasks so more of the host resources can serve EC2 workloads securely.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::recall topic::Compute_architecture topic::Virtualization

column2: A workload requires direct access to physical server hardware while retaining VPC and EBS integration. Which EC2 option fits?
column3: An EC2 bare metal instance. It provides direct access to the physical server while retaining AWS integrations.
column4:
Nitro-based bare metal provides direct hardware access within the EC2 service model.
Example: A licensing or performance workload accesses the physical processor directly while still using VPC networking and EBS.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::Compute topic::Bare_metal

column2: What is Bottlerocket?
column3: An AWS-sponsored minimal Linux-based operating system designed for hosting containers.
column4:
Its reduced package surface and transactional update model target secure container hosts.
Example: An ECS node runs Bottlerocket with a minimal software footprint focused on hosting containers.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::recall topic::Containers topic::Operating_systems

column2: What does AWS ParallelCluster automate?
column3: Creation and management of HPC clusters on AWS from configuration and command-line workflows.
column4:
It provisions components such as head and compute nodes and integrates with HPC schedulers.
Example: A researcher describes an HPC cluster in configuration, and ParallelCluster creates its scheduler, instances, and networking.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::recall topic::High-performance_computing topic::Cluster_management

column2: Tightly coupled HPC nodes need very low inter-instance latency. Which combination should be evaluated?
column3: A cluster placement group with Elastic Fabric Adapter on supported EC2 instances.
column4:
Cluster placement provides close placement in one AZ; EFA supports high-performance inter-instance communication.
Example: Simulation nodes use a cluster placement group and EFA to exchange data with very low latency.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::High-performance_computing topic::Networking

column2: Which service provides a high-performance parallel file system commonly used by HPC workloads?
column3: Amazon FSx for Lustre. It provides a high-performance parallel file system for data-intensive and HPC workloads.
column4:
FSx for Lustre is optimized for fast parallel access to large datasets.
Example: Compute nodes read and write a shared high-throughput dataset through an FSx for Lustre file system.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::scenario topic::High-performance_computing topic::Storage

column2: What does AWS Ground Station provide?
column3: Managed satellite ground-station capabilities integrated with AWS services.
column4:
It lets customers schedule satellite contacts and move received data into AWS for processing and storage.
Example: A satellite operator schedules an antenna contact and sends the received data directly into AWS services.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::recall topic::Satellite_workloads

column2: Distinguish high availability from fault tolerance without using fixed percentages.
column3: High availability minimizes downtime through redundancy and recovery; fault tolerance aims to continue operating despite component failure.
column4:
Neither term guarantees one universal SLA or literal 100% availability.
Example: A highly available service recovers quickly after a node fails; a fault-tolerant design continues serving without interruption.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_4_—_Edge,_Private_Connectivity_&_Compliance type::comparison topic::Resilience topic::Availability

column2: Distinguish RTO from RPO.
column3: RTO is maximum acceptable time to restore service; RPO is maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
column4:
RTO looks forward from disruption to recovery; RPO looks backward to the last recoverable point.
Example: An RPO of 15 minutes permits 15 minutes of lost changes, while an RTO of one hour permits one hour to restore service.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_5_—_Disaster_Recovery_&_AWS_APIs type::comparison topic::Disaster_recovery topic::Recovery_objectives

column2: Which studied DR strategy generally has the lowest ongoing cost but the longest recovery time?
column3: Backup and restore. Resources are recreated from backups after the incident, keeping ongoing cost low but recovery slower.
column4:
Infrastructure and data are restored after the event, trading low standby cost for higher RTO and often higher RPO.
Example: After a disaster, the team restores database backups and redeploys servers, accepting slower recovery for very low standby cost.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_5_—_Disaster_Recovery_&_AWS_APIs type::scenario topic::Disaster_recovery topic::Backup_and_restore

column2: What remains ready in a pilot-light disaster recovery strategy?
column3: The critical core of the workload, including replicated data, while additional application infrastructure is started or deployed during recovery.
column4:
Pilot light costs less than maintaining a fully functional scaled-down environment.
Example: The recovery Region keeps replicated data and essential core services ready, then launches the remaining application during failover.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_5_—_Disaster_Recovery_&_AWS_APIs type::recall topic::Disaster_recovery topic::Pilot_light

column2: What distinguishes warm standby from pilot light?
column3: Warm standby keeps a scaled-down but functional copy of the workload running in the recovery location.
column4:
It costs more during normal operation but normally recovers faster.
Example: Pilot light keeps only the critical core ready; warm standby keeps a scaled-down but complete application already running.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_5_—_Disaster_Recovery_&_AWS_APIs type::recall topic::Disaster_recovery topic::Warm_standby

column2: A company requires faster recovery than pilot light and accepts the cost of a small functional environment running continuously. Which strategy fits?
column3: Warm standby. A smaller but fully working copy runs continuously and scales up during recovery.
column4:
The recovery environment already serves as a functional scaled-down copy and can scale after failover.
Example: A small working environment serves minimal capacity in the recovery Region and scales up when the primary Region fails.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_5_—_Disaster_Recovery_&_AWS_APIs type::scenario topic::Disaster_recovery topic::Strategy_selection

column2: Does multi-site active/active automatically guarantee RPO 0?
column3: No. It can reduce recovery time to near zero, but RPO depends on the data architecture and replication behavior.
column4:
Data corruption may still require backups, and active traffic in multiple Regions does not prove synchronous writes.
Example: Two Regions may already serve traffic, yet asynchronous database replication can still leave the recovery copy several seconds behind.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_5_—_Disaster_Recovery_&_AWS_APIs type::recall topic::Disaster_recovery topic::Active/active

column2: How do synchronous and asynchronous replication affect RPO?
column3: Synchronous replication can target RPO 0 but adds latency and constraints; asynchronous replication can leave a replication lag.
column4:
The replication method affects data-loss exposure independently of how quickly compute recovers.
Example: A synchronous write waits for both copies and can target zero data loss; an asynchronous replica may remain several seconds behind.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_5_—_Disaster_Recovery_&_AWS_APIs type::comparison topic::Disaster_recovery topic::Replication

column2: What does AWS CloudFormation do?
column3: It provisions and manages AWS resources from declarative JSON or YAML templates.
column4:
Deployed resources are managed in stacks as logical units.
Example: The same reviewed YAML template creates an identical test environment and production environment.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::recall topic::Infrastructure_as_Code

column2: What is a CloudFormation stack?
column3: A collection of AWS resources managed as a single unit from a template.
column4:
Creating, updating, and deleting the stack manages the related resources and their dependencies.
Example: One stack manages a VPC, load balancer, and servers together, while a retained database can survive stack deletion.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::recall topic::Infrastructure_as_Code topic::Stacks

column2: Does deleting a CloudFormation stack always delete every resource it ever managed?
column3: No. Deletion policies, retained resources, dependencies, or deletion failures can leave resources behind.
column4:
CloudFormation deletes managed resources by default, but lifecycle controls and failures are important exceptions.
Example: One stack manages a VPC, load balancer, and servers together, while a retained database can survive stack deletion.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::scenario topic::Infrastructure_as_Code topic::Resource_lifecycle

column2: What happens when `cdk synth` runs?
column3: AWS CDK synthesizes the application’s constructs into a CloudFormation template.
column4:
CloudFormation remains the deployment engine for the synthesized infrastructure definition.
Example: A TypeScript CDK definition of a bucket becomes a declarative CloudFormation template when cdk synth runs.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::recall topic::Infrastructure_as_Code topic::CDK

column2: Distinguish an AWS SDK from AWS CDK.
column3: An SDK invokes AWS APIs from application or automation code; CDK defines infrastructure and synthesizes CloudFormation templates.
column4:
Use an SDK for runtime service operations and CDK for infrastructure definitions.
Example: Application code uses an SDK to upload an object; infrastructure code uses CDK to define the bucket and synthesize CloudFormation.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::comparison topic::Developer_tools topic::Infrastructure_as_Code

column2: What is an Amazon Resource Name (ARN) used for?
column3: To identify an AWS resource in APIs, policies, and service integrations using a service-specific format.
column4:
ARN segments and resource portions vary, and global-resource ARNs can omit the Region segment.
Example: An IAM policy uses a bucket ARN to grant access to exactly that resource.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_5_—_Disaster_Recovery_&_AWS_APIs type::recall topic::Resource_identifiers

column2: What does AWS Signature Version 4 provide for API requests?
column3: It authenticates the credentialed caller and protects request integrity by signing request data.
column4:
SDKs and the CLI normally create the signature automatically from credentials.
Example: The AWS CLI hashes and signs a request so AWS can verify both the caller and the request contents.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_5_—_Disaster_Recovery_&_AWS_APIs type::recall topic::API_security topic::Request_signing

column2: What is the difference between a Regional service endpoint and a global endpoint?
column3: A Regional endpoint targets service API behavior in a named Region; a global endpoint has no Region in the hostname and serves global or centralized behavior.
column4:
Endpoint scope and resource scope are related but not always identical, so avoid assuming every URL follows one rule.
Example: An EC2 API call targets a named Region such as us-west-2, while a centralized global service may expose an endpoint without a Region in its hostname.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_5_—_Disaster_Recovery_&_AWS_APIs type::comparison topic::APIs topic::Service_endpoints

column2: Why is calling AWS CDK purely “imperative IaC” incomplete?
column3: CDK code can use imperative language features, but it synthesizes a declarative CloudFormation template that CloudFormation deploys.
column4:
The source language and the deployment model are different layers.
Example: CDK code can use loops and functions, but the result deployed by CloudFormation is still a declarative template.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_6_—_CloudFormation,_CDK_&_Responsibility type::recall topic::Infrastructure_as_Code topic::CDK

column2: A company needs to decouple order processing and independently notify several subscribers. Which TWO services meet these separate needs?
column3: Use Amazon SQS for the work queue and Amazon SNS for fan-out notifications.
column4:
SQS buffers work for consumers; SNS publishes to multiple subscriptions.
Example: SQS buffers each order for one worker, while SNS independently publishes an order event to several interested subscribers.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_1_—_Cloud_Foundations_&_IaC type::multiple-response topic::Messaging topic::Service_selection

column2: Which TWO actions are recommended for the AWS account root user?
column3: Enable MFA and use root only for tasks that require it.
column4:
The root user is unrestricted and should not be used for routine work or programmatic access keys.
Example: An administrator uses a normal role every day and opens the root account only for a task that specifically requires root.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_2_—_IAM,_CloudFront_&_Monitoring type::multiple-response topic::Root_user topic::Security_best_practices

column2: A security team must explicitly deny one malicious IP range for every resource in a subnet. Which control should it configure?
column3: A network ACL. It can apply an explicit deny rule to traffic crossing the subnet boundary.
column4:
NACLs operate at subnet boundaries and support explicit deny rules; security groups are allow-only.
Example: A subnet NACL denies a known malicious CIDR and separately permits the required inbound and outbound traffic.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::single-choice topic::Network_security

column2: Which statement about VPC network scope is correct?
column3: A VPC spans Availability Zones in one Region, while each subnet belongs to one AZ.
column4:
A VPC is Regional and subnets are AZ-scoped.
Example: A company creates one public and one private subnet in each of two Availability Zones for resilience.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::single-choice topic::Networking topic::Global_infrastructure

column2: Which statement correctly describes a general-purpose S3 bucket?
column3: Its data is stored in a selected Region, while its bucket name is globally unique.
column4:
Global naming and the global console view do not make the bucket’s data automatically global.
Example: The globally unique bucket name company-receipts can still store its objects only in the selected eu-west-1 Region.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_3_—_Global_Infrastructure_&_VPC type::single-choice topic::Storage topic::Global_infrastructure

column2: Private EC2 instances need same-Region S3 access without a NAT gateway or additional endpoint charge. Which option is best?
column3: An S3 gateway VPC endpoint. It provides private S3 access through route-table entries without an hourly endpoint charge.
column4:
Gateway endpoints route S3 traffic through selected route tables with no additional endpoint charge.
Example: Private instances reach S3 through a route-table entry without using a NAT gateway.

ECS and EKS orchestrate containers; Fargate supplies managed compute capacity.

column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_7_—_Compute,_Containers,_HPC_&_Storage type::single-choice topic::Containers topic::Serverless

column2: A business can tolerate losing at most 15 minutes of transactions after a disaster. Which objective is being specified?
column3: Recovery Point Objective (RPO).
column4:
RPO expresses acceptable data loss measured in time before the disruption.

column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Concepts day::2026-08-28 chat::2026-08-28_-_Chat_5_—_Disaster_Recovery_&_AWS_APIs type::single-choice topic::Disaster_recovery topic::Recovery_objectives

column2: A recovery Region runs a small but fully functional copy of the workload and scales up after failover. Which strategy is this?

Warm standby keeps reduced-capacity functionality running continuously.
Example: A small working copy serves minimal capacity in the recovery Region and scales up when the primary Region fails.

column2: Which statement about multi-site active/active is most accurate?
column3: It can reduce RTO to near zero, but RPO still depends on the data architecture and replication behavior.

Serving traffic from several Regions does not automatically guarantee synchronous writes or zero data loss.
Example: Active/active Regions can make application failover almost immediate, but asynchronous database writes may still create a nonzero RPO.

column2: An application runs on EC2 and needs access to S3. What is the preferred credential approach?

Roles avoid embedding long-lived access keys in application files.

column2: A factory must run AWS-managed infrastructure inside its own facility for local processing. Which service is designed for this?

Outposts extends AWS infrastructure and selected services to customer premises.

column2: What is the primary purpose of Amazon RDS?
column3: To run managed relational databases using supported database engines.

AWS manages much of the database infrastructure and routine operations while the customer manages data, access, schema, and workload choices.
Example: A company runs PostgreSQL on RDS so AWS handles backups and database infrastructure while the team manages its schema and data.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Databases topic::Relational_databases

column2: Name four database engines supported by Amazon RDS.
column3: Any four of PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server, and IBM Db2.
column4:
RDS is a managed service layer for familiar relational engines.
Example: A company runs PostgreSQL on RDS so AWS handles backups and database infrastructure while the team manages its schema and data.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Databases topic::Amazon_RDS

column2: A company wants to move an existing Microsoft SQL Server application to a managed AWS database with minimal application change. Which service should it evaluate first?
column3: Amazon RDS for SQL Server.
column4:
RDS supports familiar commercial and open-source engines, making it suitable for many lift-and-shift relational migrations.
Example: A legacy application keeps Microsoft SQL Server while moving to RDS so AWS manages backups and database infrastructure.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::Databases topic::Migration

column2: What is Amazon Aurora?
column3: An AWS-built relational database engine compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL.
column4:
Aurora is cloud-native rather than a hosted copy of the MySQL or PostgreSQL engine.
Example: A new payment application uses Aurora PostgreSQL for relational SQL with storage designed to remain available across multiple AZs.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Databases topic::Aurora

column2: How does Aurora differ from the other engines available through Amazon RDS?
column3: Aurora is an AWS-built cloud-native engine; the other RDS choices are existing third-party or open-source engines.
column4:
Both are managed relational options, but their engine origins and architectures differ.
Example: Choose Aurora for an AWS-built MySQL-compatible design; choose RDS for SQL Server when the application must keep the Microsoft engine.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::comparison topic::Databases topic::Relational_databases

column2: Across how many Availability Zones does Aurora store copies of data in a typical Aurora cluster?
column3: Three Availability Zones.
column4:
Aurora’s distributed storage maintains copies across three AZs for durability and availability.
Example: A new payment application uses Aurora PostgreSQL for relational SQL with storage designed to remain available across multiple AZs.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Databases topic::High_availability

column2: A new relational workload needs MySQL compatibility and an AWS-built, highly available cloud-native engine. Which service fits?
column3: Amazon Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition. It combines MySQL compatibility with AWS-designed distributed storage.
column4:
Aurora combines familiar MySQL or PostgreSQL compatibility with an AWS-designed distributed architecture.
Example: A new application keeps the MySQL protocol but uses Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition for an AWS-built relational design.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::Databases topic::Service_selection

column3: Amazon RDS for Oracle. It preserves the Oracle engine while AWS manages much of the database infrastructure.

Aurora supports MySQL and PostgreSQL compatibility, not the Oracle engine.

column3: Data warehousing and large-scale analytical SQL workloads.

Redshift supports OLAP and business-intelligence analysis over large datasets.

column3: Amazon Redshift. It is designed for analytical SQL and data-warehouse reporting over large datasets.

This is an analytical data-warehouse workload rather than an operational transaction database workload.
Example: A retailer loads years of sales data into Redshift so analysts can run large business-intelligence reports.

column2: What is the exam-level distinction between Amazon RDS and Amazon Redshift?
column3: RDS serves relational operational workloads; Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics.

The distinction is primarily OLTP-style application work versus OLAP-style analysis.
Example: An application records individual orders in RDS, then analysts summarize years of order history in a Redshift warehouse.

Keeping frequently accessed data in memory can lower latency and reduce load on backing databases.

column3: Amazon ElastiCache. It keeps frequently requested results in memory so the application makes fewer database reads.
column4:
Frequently accessed results can be served from memory instead of repeatedly querying the database.
Example: A catalog page reads popular product details from memory instead of querying the database on every visit.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::Caching topic::Performance

column2: Which THREE engines are current Amazon ElastiCache choices?
column3: Valkey, Memcached, and Redis OSS.

The service is not limited to only the two engines historically emphasized in older learning material.
Example: An application can choose Valkey or Redis OSS for feature-rich caching, or Memcached for a simpler distributed cache.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::multiple-response topic::Caching topic::Engines

column3: Amazon Neptune. Its graph model is designed to traverse relationships among highly connected entities.

The core requirement is exploring a highly connected graph of entities.

column3: Amazon Timestream for LiveAnalytics. It stores and analyzes measurements organized by time.

column3: Amazon Timestream for LiveAnalytics. It stores and analyzes measurements organized by time.

Redshift can analyze large datasets, but Timestream is purpose-built for time-series measurements.
Example: Millions of devices write timestamped readings to Timestream so operators can query how measurements changed over time.

column2: What is the primary purpose of AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS)?
column3: To migrate or replicate databases to AWS with minimal downtime.
column4:
DMS supports both homogeneous and heterogeneous database moves.
Example: A company copies its on-premises database to AWS while ongoing changes continue to replicate until cutover.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Migration topic::Databases

column2: A company must keep its source database available while continuously replicating changes during migration to AWS. Which service fits?
column3: AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS). It copies and can continuously replicate database data to reduce migration downtime.
column4:
DMS can perform an initial load and ongoing change replication to reduce migration downtime.
Example: A company copies its on-premises database to AWS while ongoing changes continue to replicate until cutover.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::Migration topic::Databases

column2: Why might a heterogeneous DMS migration need schema conversion?
column3: Different database engines can use different schema objects, data types, and SQL features.
column4:
DMS moves data, but engine differences may require a separate schema-conversion step.
Example: An Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration converts incompatible table definitions and stored code before DMS moves the data.
