column2: Can one Amazon VPC span Regions or Availability Zones?
column3: It can span Availability Zones within one Region, but it cannot span Regions.
column4:
Subnets provide AZ-level partitions inside the Regional VPC.
Example: A VPC in us-east-1 can contain subnets in us-east-1a and us-east-1b, but it cannot extend into us-west-2.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Networking topic::VPC_scope

column2: Can a subnet span multiple Availability Zones?
column3: No. A subnet belongs to exactly one Availability Zone.
column4:
An AZ may contain multiple subnets, but a subnet cannot cross AZ boundaries.
Example: A company creates one public and one private subnet in each of two Availability Zones for resilience.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Networking topic::Subnets

column2: What routing property distinguishes a public subnet from a private subnet?
column3: A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway; a private subnet has no direct route to an internet gateway.
column4:
Public addressing and security rules are additional requirements for an instance to communicate directly with the internet.
Example: A web subnet has a default route to an internet gateway; a database subnet has no direct internet-gateway route.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::comparison topic::Networking topic::Subnets

column2: An EC2 instance is in a subnet with a route to an internet gateway but has only a private IPv4 address. Is it directly reachable from the internet over IPv4?
column3: No. It also needs a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP and traffic must be allowed by security controls.
column4:
A public-subnet route alone does not give the instance a public address or open firewall rules.
Example: A public web server needs a public IP, a route to the internet gateway, and security rules allowing HTTPS.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::Networking topic::Public_subnets

column2: What does an internet gateway do?
column3: It enables communication between a VPC and the internet when routing, addressing, and security rules permit it.
column4:
An internet gateway is a managed, redundant, highly available VPC component.
Example: A public web server needs a public IP, a route to the internet gateway, and security rules allowing HTTPS.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Networking topic::Internet_gateway

column2: Private-subnet EC2 instances need outbound IPv4 access for operating-system updates without accepting internet-initiated connections. What should be used?
column3: A NAT gateway, with the private subnet routed to it. This gives private instances outbound IPv4 access without accepting new inbound internet sessions.
column4:
The NAT gateway initiates outbound translation and permits return traffic, but not unsolicited inbound sessions.
Example: Private application servers download operating-system updates through a NAT gateway but cannot receive unsolicited internet connections.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::Networking topic::NAT_gateway

column2: What is the core difference between an internet gateway and a NAT gateway?
column3: An internet gateway supports direct internet connectivity for publicly addressed resources; a NAT gateway gives private resources outbound connectivity through address translation.
column4:
They serve different routing and addressing patterns and are not interchangeable.
Example: A publicly addressed web server connects directly through an internet gateway; a private server downloads updates through a NAT gateway.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::comparison topic::Networking topic::Gateways

column2: What information does a VPC route-table rule contain?
column3: A destination and a target.
column4:
The most specific matching destination determines where traffic is sent.
Example: The rule 0.0.0.0/0 → internet gateway pairs the destination range with the component that receives matching traffic.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Networking topic::Route_tables

column2: Do VPC route tables assign IP addresses or act as firewalls?
column3: No. They select network paths; address configuration and traffic filtering are separate functions.
column4:
DHCP-related settings help configure hosts, while security groups and NACLs filter traffic.
Example: A route table sends traffic toward an internet gateway; a security group separately decides whether HTTPS is allowed.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Networking topic::Route_tables

column2: What is the purpose of the local route in a VPC route table?
column3: It enables communication among resources within the VPC CIDR blocks.
column4:
Every VPC route table contains local routing for intra-VPC communication.
Example: Traffic for 10.0.2.15 follows the 10.0.0.0/16 local route instead of the less-specific 0.0.0.0/0 route.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Networking topic::Local_route

column2: A route table has 10.0.0.0/16 → local and 0.0.0.0/0 → internet gateway. Where does traffic for 10.0.2.15 go?
column3: Through the local route. The VPC’s /16 route is more specific than the /0 internet route.
column4:
Route selection uses the most specific matching destination; /16 is more specific than /0.
Example: Traffic for 10.0.2.15 chooses the 10.0.0.0/16 local route because /16 is more specific than the /0 internet route.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::Networking topic::Route_selection

column2: What role do DHCP options play in a VPC?
column3: They provide network configuration such as DNS-related settings to instances.
column4:
DHCP configuration is separate from the subnet route table, which selects traffic paths.
Example: A VPC DHCP options set supplies DNS settings to a newly launched EC2 instance.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Networking topic::DHCP

column2: At what level does a security group apply, and is it stateful?
column3: It applies to supported resource network interfaces and is stateful.
column4:
Allowed flow responses are automatically permitted, and security groups contain allow rules rather than deny rules.
Example: A web server security group permits inbound HTTPS, and the response traffic is allowed automatically.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Network_security topic::Security_groups

column2: At what level does a network ACL apply, and is it stateful?
column3: It applies at the subnet boundary and is stateless.
column4:
Inbound and outbound rules are evaluated separately, and NACLs support both allow and deny rules.
Example: A subnet NACL denies a known malicious CIDR and separately permits the required inbound and outbound traffic.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Network_security topic::Network_ACLs

column2: Contrast security groups with network ACLs.
column3: Security groups are stateful allow-only controls on resource ENIs; NACLs are stateless allow/deny controls at subnet boundaries.
column4:
They can be used together for layered protection.
Example: A security group allows HTTPS to one server and automatically permits replies; a subnet NACL separately allows or denies both traffic directions.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::comparison topic::Network_security

column2: A security group allows an inbound HTTPS request. Does the response require a separate outbound rule for that flow?
column3: No. Return traffic is automatically allowed because the security group is stateful.
column4:
State tracking recognizes response traffic for an allowed connection.
Example: A web server security group permits inbound HTTPS, and the response traffic is allowed automatically.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::Network_security topic::Stateful_filtering

column2: A NACL allows an inbound request. What must be considered for the response?
column3: An applicable outbound rule must also allow the response traffic.
column4:
NACLs are stateless and evaluate each direction independently.
Example: A subnet NACL denies a known malicious CIDR and separately permits the required inbound and outbound traffic.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::Network_security topic::Stateless_filtering

column2: Can one security group be associated with resources in different subnets of the same VPC?
column3: Yes. A security group is associated with resource network interfaces, not owned by one subnet.
column4:
The same group can protect supported resources across multiple subnets in its VPC.
Example: The same WebServers security group can protect EC2 instances in two different subnets of the same VPC.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Network_security topic::Security_groups

column2: Which VPC control can explicitly deny a malicious source CIDR at a subnet boundary?
column3: A network ACL. It can apply an explicit deny rule to traffic crossing the subnet boundary.
column4:
Security groups do not contain deny rules; NACLs can allow or deny and apply to the subnet boundary.
Example: A subnet NACL denies a known malicious CIDR and separately permits the required inbound and outbound traffic.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::single-choice topic::Network_security topic::Explicit_deny

column2: What problem does a VPC endpoint solve?
column3: It lets resources privately access supported services without requiring public internet connectivity.
column4:
The client does not need an internet gateway, NAT device, VPN, or public IP for that service path.
Example: A private EC2 instance reaches a supported AWS service through a VPC endpoint without a public IP, NAT gateway, or internet gateway.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Private_connectivity topic::VPC_endpoints

column2: How is an interface VPC endpoint implemented?
column3: With endpoint network interfaces that have private IP addresses in selected subnets, powered by AWS PrivateLink.
column4:
Security groups can control access to the endpoint interfaces, and endpoint charges normally apply.
Example: A private application reaches Secrets Manager through private endpoint IP addresses protected by a security group.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Private_connectivity topic::Interface_endpoints

column2: Which services support gateway VPC endpoints?
column3: Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB.
column4:
Gateway endpoints add routes to selected route tables and do not use AWS PrivateLink.
Example: A VPC can add route-table-based gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB; other services generally use interface endpoints.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::Private_connectivity topic::Gateway_endpoints

column2: How do interface and gateway VPC endpoints differ?
column3: Interface endpoints use PrivateLink ENIs with private IPs; gateway endpoints add route-table entries and support S3 and DynamoDB.
column4:
The endpoint types differ in implementation, supported services, security integration, and pricing.
Example: Private S3 traffic can use a gateway endpoint route, while private Secrets Manager traffic can use an interface endpoint ENI.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::comparison topic::Private_connectivity topic::VPC_endpoints

column2: Private EC2 instances need same-Region S3 access without NAT and without an endpoint-hour charge. Which endpoint is the usual choice?
column3: An S3 gateway VPC endpoint. It provides private S3 access through route-table entries without an hourly endpoint charge.
column4:
Gateway endpoints add S3 routes and have no additional endpoint charge.
Example: Private instances reach S3 through a route-table entry without using a NAT gateway.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::Private_connectivity topic::Amazon_S3

column2: A private subnet must access a supported AWS service through private IP addresses and control access with a security group. Which endpoint type fits?
column3: An interface VPC endpoint. It creates private-IP network interfaces that can be protected with security groups.
column4:
Interface endpoints create ENIs in selected subnets and can have security groups.
Example: A private application reaches Secrets Manager through an interface endpoint’s private IPs and restricts access with its security group.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::Private_connectivity topic::Interface_endpoints

column2: Which statement is correct?
column3: A DynamoDB gateway endpoint uses route-table entries and does not use AWS PrivateLink.
column4:
Interface endpoints use PrivateLink; S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints use a different route-table implementation.
Example: A DynamoDB gateway endpoint adds service routes to selected route tables instead of creating PrivateLink network interfaces.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::single-choice topic::Private_connectivity topic::VPC_endpoints

column2: Which EC2 category balances compute, memory, and networking for diverse workloads?
column3: General purpose instances, with families such as T and M.
column4:
Use workload characteristics rather than treating family letters as official acronym expansions.
Example: A general-purpose M family instance fits a web application that needs a balanced mix of CPU, memory, and networking.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::recall topic::EC2 topic::Instance_categories

column2: A batch-processing workload is CPU intensive. Which EC2 category should be evaluated?
column3: Compute optimized instances, such as C families.
column4:
These instances provide a higher ratio of compute resources for CPU-bound work.
Example: A CPU-heavy media-encoding job uses a C family instance.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::EC2 topic::Compute_optimized

column2: An in-memory database needs very large RAM capacity. Which EC2 category fits?
column3: Memory optimized instances, such as R or X families.
column4:
The workload is constrained primarily by memory rather than CPU or local disk.
Example: A large in-memory database uses an R family instance because RAM is the main constraint.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::EC2 topic::Memory_optimized

column2: A machine-learning training workload needs GPUs. Which EC2 category fits?
column3: Accelerated computing instances, such as P or G families.
column4:
Hardware accelerators handle specialized operations more efficiently than general-purpose CPUs.
Example: A machine-learning training job uses GPU-backed P family instances to accelerate matrix calculations.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::EC2 topic::Accelerated_computing

column2: A workload needs very high local NVMe IOPS. Which EC2 category should be evaluated?
column3: Storage optimized instances, such as I families.
column4:
These instances are designed for workloads whose performance depends on local storage throughput or IOPS.
Example: A high-IOPS local database evaluates an I family instance with NVMe instance storage.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::EC2 topic::Storage_optimized

column2: Contrast Shared tenancy, Dedicated Instances, and Dedicated Hosts.
column3: Shared is multi-account hardware by default; Dedicated Instances use single-account hardware without host control; Dedicated Hosts give one customer an entire physical server with host visibility and placement control.
column4:
Tenancy describes how physical infrastructure is allocated.
Example: A normal server uses shared tenancy, a compliance workload may use Dedicated Instances, and a socket-bound license uses a Dedicated Host.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::comparison topic::EC2 topic::Tenancy

column2: A license is bound to physical sockets and cores and requires host-level auditing. Which EC2 tenancy option is the best fit?
column3: A Dedicated Host. It exposes the physical host, sockets, and cores needed for server-bound licensing.
column4:
Dedicated Hosts expose host identity, sockets, and cores and support targeted placement for server-bound licensing scenarios.
Example: A database license tied to physical sockets runs on a Dedicated Host so the company can audit cores and host placement.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::scenario topic::EC2 topic::BYOL

column2: How does EC2 tenancy differ from EC2 purchasing models?
column3: Tenancy describes physical hardware sharing or dedication; purchasing models describe price, interruption, or commitment.
column4:
Dedicated Host and Dedicated Instance answer an isolation question, while On-Demand, Spot, Reserved Instances, and Savings Plans answer cost-model questions.
Example: A server can use dedicated tenancy for isolation while also using an On-Demand or commitment-based purchase option for cost.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-01 chat::2026-09-01_-_Chat_8_—_Databases,_VPC_&_EC2 type::comparison topic::EC2 topic::Pricing topic::Tenancy

column2: How do a Regional Reserved Instance and a Zonal Reserved Instance differ?
column3: A Regional RI provides a billing discount across a Region but no capacity reservation. A Zonal RI applies in one Availability Zone and reserves matching capacity there.
column4:
Separate the discount from the promise of capacity: only the Zonal RI includes both.
Example: A company expecting steady use anywhere in us-east-1 may choose Regional; one that must launch in us-east-1a may choose Zonal.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::comparison topic::EC2_pricing topic::Reserved_Instances

column2: Does buying a Regional Reserved Instance create or reserve an EC2 instance?
column3: No. It is a billing benefit that AWS automatically applies to matching running usage.
column4:
The instance still runs as normal EC2 capacity; the RI changes how eligible usage is billed.
Example: Buying ten Regional RIs does not launch ten servers.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::recall topic::EC2_pricing topic::Reserved_Instances

column2: A workload must be able to launch in one specific Availability Zone during a capacity shortage. Which option directly reserves that capacity?
column3: A Zonal Reserved Instance or an On-Demand Capacity Reservation.
column4:
Both reserve matching EC2 capacity in a particular Availability Zone; a Regional RI does not.
Example: A disaster-recovery server must be guaranteed space in us-west-2b.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::scenario topic::EC2_pricing topic::Capacity

column2: What happens financially when an On-Demand Capacity Reservation is unused?
column3: You still pay for the reserved capacity.
column4:
AWS sets that capacity aside for you, so an unused reservation is billed much like an unused running instance.
Example: Reserving capacity for five instances and running only three leaves two billed but unused slots.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::recall topic::EC2_pricing topic::Capacity_Reservations

column2: When is a Standard RI generally preferable to a Convertible RI?
column3: Choose Standard when the workload is predictable and the priority is a larger discount; choose Convertible when future instance needs may change.
column4:
Convertible RIs allow exchanges for different eligible configurations, trading some discount for flexibility.
Example: A stable production server favors Standard; a growing workload that may change families may favor Convertible.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::comparison topic::EC2_pricing topic::Reserved_Instances

column2: A batch-rendering job can stop and restart without harming the business. Which EC2 purchase option is usually most economical?
column3: Spot Instances.
column4:
Spot uses spare EC2 capacity at a steep discount, but AWS can interrupt it. The application must tolerate interruptions.
Example: A renderer checkpoints each frame and resumes on another instance.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::scenario topic::EC2_pricing topic::Spot_Instances

column2: What is the key difference between Savings Plans and Reserved Instances at exam level?
column3: Savings Plans commit to an hourly amount of eligible usage; RIs provide a discount for matching instance attributes and may be Regional or Zonal.
column4:
Both reduce cost for predictable use, but they define the commitment differently.
Example: A Compute Savings Plan can follow eligible compute changes more flexibly than a Standard EC2 RI.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::comparison topic::EC2_pricing topic::Savings_Plans

column2: What four Savings Plans types does AWS currently document?
column3: Compute, EC2 Instance, SageMaker AI, and Database Savings Plans.
column4:
Older study material may list fewer types. The durable idea is that each plan discounts a defined family of eligible usage.
Example: A Database Savings Plan can apply to eligible database usage rather than EC2 compute.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::recall topic::Pricing topic::Savings_Plans

column2: A company must track physical sockets and cores for server-bound software licenses. Which EC2 tenancy option fits?
column3: A Dedicated Host.
column4:
A Dedicated Host gives visibility and control over a physical server. Dedicated Instances isolate hardware but abstract the host details.
Example: A license is valid only for a named physical socket count.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::scenario topic::EC2_tenancy topic::Licensing

column2: How do Dedicated Instances differ from Dedicated Hosts?
column3: Both isolate hardware to one customer, but Dedicated Hosts expose and control the physical host; Dedicated Instances do not.
column4:
Dedicated Instances can move between AWS-controlled hosts, while a Dedicated Host is an allocated physical server.
Example: General compliance isolation may use Dedicated Instances; strict host-bound licensing uses a Dedicated Host.
column5: CLF-C02 Billing, Pricing, and Support day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::comparison topic::EC2_tenancy

column2: What does an IAM policy Condition do?
column3: It narrows when a policy statement applies.
column4:
Conditions can require context such as MFA, a source IP, a resource tag, or a time range.
Example: Allow an action only when the request comes through MFA.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::recall topic::IAM topic::Policies

column2: Do service control policies grant permissions to users or roles?
column3: No. SCPs set the maximum permissions available in member accounts; an IAM policy must still grant the action.
column4:
An action must be allowed by the organization boundary and by the relevant identity or resource policy.
Example: An SCP allows S3, but a role with no S3 permission still cannot read a bucket.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::recall topic::Organizations topic::SCPs

column2: How do CloudTrail, GuardDuty, and Detective work together?
column3: CloudTrail records activity, GuardDuty detects suspicious behavior, and Detective helps investigate relationships and timelines.
column4:
They answer different questions: what happened, is it suspicious, and how is it connected?
Example: GuardDuty raises a credential-abuse finding; Detective helps trace the related resources and events.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::comparison topic::Security_monitoring

column2: What threats do AWS WAF and AWS Shield primarily address?
column3: WAF filters malicious web requests; Shield protects against distributed denial-of-service attacks.
column4:
WAF uses web-layer rules such as IP, path, or SQL-injection patterns. Shield focuses on DDoS resilience.
Example: Block a bad HTTP request with WAF; absorb a traffic flood with Shield.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::comparison topic::Security topic::Edge_protection

column2: What is the primary purpose of AWS KMS?
column3: To create and control encryption keys used to protect data.
column4:
KMS integrates with many AWS services and records key usage through CloudTrail.
Example: An S3 bucket can use a KMS key for server-side encryption.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::recall topic::Encryption

column2: Employees need one workforce sign-in for several AWS accounts. Which service should be evaluated?
column3: AWS IAM Identity Center.
column4:
It centrally assigns workforce access to AWS accounts and supported applications.
Example: A developer signs in once and selects the development or production account.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_9_—_EC2_Pricing_&_Security type::scenario topic::Identity topic::Multi-account

column2: What does a container package?
column3: An application together with the libraries and dependencies it needs to run consistently.
column4:
Containers make the application portable across environments that support the container runtime.
Example: The same image can run on a laptop and later as an ECS task.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::recall topic::Containers

column2: What is a Kubernetes Pod?
column3: The smallest deployable Kubernetes unit, containing one or more closely related containers.
column4:
Containers in a Pod share networking and can share storage; the exam does not require Dockerfile syntax.
Example: A web container and a tightly coupled logging sidecar can share one Pod.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::recall topic::Containers topic::Kubernetes

column2: When should you choose Amazon ECS instead of Amazon EKS?
column3: Choose ECS for AWS-native container orchestration; choose EKS when the workload or team specifically needs Kubernetes compatibility.
column4:
ECS and EKS both schedule containers, but EKS exposes the Kubernetes ecosystem and APIs.
Example: A team already using Kubernetes manifests may prefer EKS; an AWS-only team may prefer ECS simplicity.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::comparison topic::Containers topic::Orchestration

column2: What does AWS Fargate remove from container operations?
column3: The need to provision and manage the underlying servers.
column4:
Fargate provides serverless compute capacity for ECS or EKS; you still define and operate the containers.
Example: An ECS task runs without the team creating an EC2 cluster.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::recall topic::Containers topic::Serverless

column2: What is stored in Amazon ECR?
column3: Container images.
column4:
ECR is a managed image registry. ECS or EKS can pull images from it to run containers.
Example: A CI pipeline pushes version 2.1 of an application image to ECR.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::recall topic::Containers topic::Registry

column2: How do Elastic Beanstalk and Lightsail differ?
column3: Elastic Beanstalk manages application deployment on configurable AWS resources; Lightsail provides simplified, predictable bundles for small workloads.
column4:
Beanstalk offers more access to underlying AWS services, while Lightsail reduces choices and setup.
Example: A small brochure site may use Lightsail; a web app needing autoscaling policies may use Beanstalk.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::comparison topic::Application_deployment

column2: How do AWS Amplify and Elastic Beanstalk differ?
column3: Amplify focuses on web/mobile frontend development and hosting; Beanstalk deploys general web applications on managed AWS infrastructure.
column4:
The service choice follows the developer experience and application type.
Example: A React frontend with managed hosting fits Amplify; a Java web service may fit Beanstalk.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::comparison topic::Application_deployment

column2: A distributed application is slow, and the team needs to see which service call causes the delay. Which service helps?
column3: AWS X-Ray.
column4:
X-Ray traces a request as it moves through application components and shows latency and errors.
Example: A checkout request spends two seconds in one downstream API.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::scenario topic::Observability topic::Tracing

column2: What is the difference between an IAM user and an AWS member account?
column3: An IAM user is an identity inside one AWS account; a member account is an independent AWS account governed through Organizations.
column4:
Member accounts have separate resources and security boundaries. IAM users share their account context.
Example: Creating an IAM user named dev does not create a development AWS account.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::comparison topic::Organizations topic::IAM

column2: What is an organizational unit in AWS Organizations?
column3: A logical group of AWS accounts used to organize and apply governance.
column4:
OUs can be nested and can receive policies such as SCPs.
Example: Production accounts can be grouped under a Production OU.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::recall topic::Organizations topic::OUs

column2: Where should ordinary production workloads run in an AWS Organization?
column3: In member accounts, not the management account.
column4:
Keeping the management account focused on billing and organization administration reduces risk and follows AWS best practice.
Example: The ecommerce application runs in a Production member account.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::scenario topic::Organizations topic::Best_practices

column2: How do AWS Organizations and AWS Control Tower differ?
column3: Organizations provides the multi-account hierarchy and policies; Control Tower builds an opinionated governed landing zone on top of it.
column4:
Control Tower combines Organizations with account provisioning, controls, and centralized governance.
Example: Use Organizations for the account structure; add Control Tower for standardized account setup and ongoing governance.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::comparison topic::Governance topic::Multi-account

column2: What is a landing zone in AWS Control Tower?
column3: A ready-to-use, governed multi-account environment.
column4:
It establishes foundational accounts, organizational structure, logging, and controls.
Example: A company starts with separate audit, log archive, and workload accounts.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::recall topic::Governance topic::Control_Tower

column2: What does Account Factory do in AWS Control Tower?
column3: It provisions standardized AWS accounts using approved configurations.
column4:
This makes new accounts repeatable instead of manually rebuilding governance each time.
Example: A team requests a sandbox account with the company network baseline.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::recall topic::Governance topic::Control_Tower

column2: What are preventive, detective, and proactive Control Tower controls?
column3: Preventive controls block disallowed actions; detective controls report noncompliance; proactive controls check resources before deployment.
column4:
AWS now uses the term controls; guardrail is an older synonym.
Example: Denying public S3 settings is preventive; flagging drift is detective; rejecting a bad template before creation is proactive.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::comparison topic::Governance topic::Controls

column2: How do CloudWatch, CloudTrail, and AWS Config differ?
column3: CloudWatch monitors behavior, CloudTrail records API activity, and Config tracks resource configuration and compliance.
column4:
They answer how it runs, who changed it, and what configuration exists over time.
Example: An alarm fires in CloudWatch; CloudTrail names the caller; Config shows the security group before and after.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_10_—_Containers_&_Multi-Account_Governance type::comparison topic::Observability topic::Audit

column2: What are AWS resource tags?
column3: Key-value labels attached to resources for organization, cost allocation, automation, and access control.
column4:
Tags are flexible metadata, not relational rows with joins and constraints.
Example: Tag an EC2 instance Environment=Production and CostCenter=42.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::recall topic::Tagging

column2: What is the purpose of AWS Resource Groups?
column3: To create a logical view of related resources selected by tags or queries.
column4:
A group helps operate resources together even when they are different service types.
Example: Show all resources tagged Application=Payments in one group.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::recall topic::Tagging topic::Resource_organization

column2: How do the AWS CAF and Well-Architected Framework differ?
column3: CAF guides organization-wide cloud transformation; Well-Architected evaluates how a workload is designed and operated.
column4:
CAF is about adoption across people, governance, business, platform, security, and operations. Well-Architected uses six workload pillars.
Example: Executives plan a migration program with CAF; architects review a payment workload with Well-Architected.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::comparison topic::Cloud_adoption topic::Architecture

column2: How do EC2 key pairs, IAM access keys, and resource tags differ?
column3: EC2 key pairs authenticate operating-system login, IAM access keys sign AWS API requests, and tags label resources.
column4:
They solve three unrelated problems: machine login, programmatic AWS identity, and organization.
Example: SSH uses a private key; a CLI uses an access key; Cost Explorer can group by tag.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::comparison topic::Identity topic::Tagging

column2: A company needs a cloud contact center for customer calls and chat. Which service fits?
column3: Amazon Connect.
column4:
Connect provides contact-center capabilities such as routing, queues, and agent experiences.
Example: Customers call a support number and are routed to available agents.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::scenario topic::Business_applications

column2: Employees need centrally managed virtual Windows desktops. Which service fits?
column3: Amazon WorkSpaces.
column4:
WorkSpaces delivers managed virtual desktops without the company operating a traditional VDI platform.

SES is designed for scalable application email sending and receiving.

column2: Business users need interactive dashboards over company data. Which AWS service fits?
column3: Amazon QuickSight.

QuickSight is AWS managed business-intelligence and visualization service.

column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::scenario topic::Analytics topic::Business_intelligence

column2: How do CloudFormation and AWS CDK relate?
column3: CloudFormation deploys declarative infrastructure templates; CDK lets you define infrastructure in code and synthesizes a CloudFormation template.

CDK changes how the template is authored, while CloudFormation remains the deployment engine.
Example: A TypeScript CDK stack becomes a CloudFormation template before deployment.

column2: How do Elastic Beanstalk and App Runner differ?
column3: Beanstalk offers managed deployment with more access to underlying AWS resources; App Runner provides a simpler path from source or container image to a managed web service.
column4:
Both reduce operational work, but App Runner hides more infrastructure choices.
Example: A containerized HTTP API with minimal operations fits App Runner.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::comparison topic::Application_deployment

column2: What is the difference between AWS Marketplace and AWS Architecture Center?
column3: Marketplace offers third-party software and services to acquire and deploy; Architecture Center provides patterns, reference architectures, and guidance.
column4:
One is a catalog of offerings; the other is a learning and design resource.
Example: Buy a firewall appliance in Marketplace; study a three-tier reference architecture in Architecture Center.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::comparison topic::AWS_resources

column2: What does AWS License Manager help control?
column3: Software license usage across AWS and on-premises environments.
column4:
It can track license rules such as cores, sockets, or instances to reduce compliance risk.
Example: Prevent launching more licensed database servers than the contract permits.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::recall topic::Governance topic::Licensing

column2: An analyst wants to run SQL directly over CSV and Parquet files in Amazon S3 without managing servers. Which service fits?
column3: Amazon Athena.
column4:
Athena is a serverless interactive query service for data in S3.
Example: Run a SQL query over one year of access logs stored in S3.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::scenario topic::Analytics

column2: When would you choose DynamoDB, DocumentDB, Keyspaces, or Redshift?
column3: DynamoDB for serverless key-value/document access, DocumentDB for MongoDB-compatible documents, Keyspaces for Cassandra-compatible workloads, and Redshift for analytical warehousing.

The exam usually provides a data model or compatibility clue.
Example: A Cassandra migration points to Keyspaces; a BI warehouse points to Redshift.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::comparison topic::Databases

column2: How do AWS Glue and Lake Formation differ?
column3: Glue discovers, catalogs, and transforms data; Lake Formation helps build and centrally govern a data lake.
column4:
They often work together: Glue supplies metadata and ETL, while Lake Formation manages data-lake permissions and governance.
Example: A crawler catalogs S3 data, then Lake Formation controls which analysts can access it.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::comparison topic::Analytics topic::Data_lakes

column2: What does Amazon MSK manage?
column3: Apache Kafka clusters.
column4:
MSK is for applications that need the Kafka ecosystem without operating the brokers themselves.
Example: An existing Kafka event platform moves to managed brokers on AWS.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::recall topic::Streaming

column2: What is AWS Data Exchange used for?
column3: Finding, subscribing to, and using third-party data products.
column4:
Providers publish datasets and subscribers access them under defined terms.
Example: A risk team subscribes to a commercial weather dataset.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_11_—_AWS_Portfolio_&_Operations type::recall topic::Data topic::Marketplace

column2: How do Amazon Athena and AWS Glue differ?
column3: Athena queries data with SQL; Glue discovers, catalogs, and transforms data.
column4:
Athena is the query engine. Glue prepares metadata and data pipelines that Athena and other analytics services can use.
Example: Glue catalogs S3 files, then Athena queries the cataloged table.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::comparison topic::Analytics

column2: What does an AWS Glue crawler do?
column3: It scans data sources, infers their structure, and creates or updates metadata in the Glue Data Catalog.
column4:
The crawler does not primarily analyze business results; it makes datasets discoverable as tables and schemas.
Example: A crawler recognizes Parquet columns in S3 and adds a table to the catalog.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::recall topic::Analytics topic::Metadata

column2: What does ETL mean?
column3: Extract data from sources, transform it into a useful form, and load it into a destination.
column4:
ETL is a data-processing pattern, not a specific AWS product.
Example: Read sales files, clean currency fields, and write analytics-ready Parquet data.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::recall topic::Analytics topic::ETL

column2: What is a worker in an AWS Glue ETL job?
column3: Compute capacity that executes the data-processing job.
column4:
Workers provide CPU and memory for the job; they are not human operators.
Example: A larger transformation may need more or larger workers.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::recall topic::Analytics topic::ETL

column2: What is the difference between RPO and RTO?
column3: RPO is how much data loss is acceptable, measured in time; RTO is how long service restoration may take.
column4:
RPO looks backward to the latest usable data. RTO looks forward to returning the service to operation.
Example: An RPO of 15 minutes allows 15 minutes of lost updates; an RTO of one hour allows an hour to recover.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::comparison topic::Disaster_recovery

column2: Order the four common AWS disaster-recovery strategies from lowest cost/slowest recovery to highest cost/fastest recovery.
column3: Backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active/active.
column4:
Keeping more of the recovery environment continuously running generally shortens recovery but increases cost.
Example: A pilot light keeps only critical cores alive; warm standby keeps a scaled-down full environment.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::comparison topic::Disaster_recovery

column2: A company accepts hours of downtime and wants the cheapest disaster-recovery strategy. Which approach fits?
column3: Backup and restore.
column4:
Resources can be rebuilt from backups after a disaster, minimizing steady-state cost but increasing recovery time.
Example: Restore a database snapshot and redeploy infrastructure after an outage.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::scenario topic::Disaster_recovery

column2: Why are AWS API requests signed?
column3: So AWS can authenticate the caller and verify the request has not been altered.
column4:
The signature is evaluated together with IAM authorization.
Example: The AWS CLI signs a request using configured credentials before calling an API endpoint.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::recall topic::APIs topic::Security

column2: What is an Amazon Resource Name (ARN)?
column3: A standardized identifier that uniquely names an AWS resource.
column4:
Policies and APIs use ARNs to refer precisely to resources.
Example: An IAM policy can name one specific S3 bucket ARN.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::recall topic::AWS_fundamentals

column2: How do gateway and interface VPC endpoints differ?
column3: Gateway endpoints use route-table entries and support S3 and DynamoDB; interface endpoints use PrivateLink and private-IP network interfaces for many services.
column4:
Both provide private service access, but their implementation and supported services differ.
Example: A private subnet reaches S3 through a gateway endpoint and Secrets Manager through an interface endpoint.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::comparison topic::Networking topic::Private_connectivity

column2: How do Amazon SQS and Amazon SNS differ?
column3: SQS stores messages in a queue for consumers to pull; SNS pushes each publication to subscribed endpoints.
column4:
SQS decouples work and lets consumers process at their pace. SNS is useful for fan-out.
Example: An order enters an SQS worker queue; one alarm is sent by SNS to email, Lambda, and SQS.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::comparison topic::Application_integration topic::Messaging

column2: How does Amazon Kinesis differ from Amazon SQS?
column3: Kinesis is a real-time data stream that can retain ordered records for multiple readers; SQS is a work queue where messages are processed and removed.
column4:
Choose based on stream analytics versus decoupled task processing.
Example: Clickstream analytics uses Kinesis; image-resize jobs use SQS.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::comparison topic::Application_integration topic::Streaming

column2: When is Amazon MQ a better fit than Amazon SQS?
column3: When migrating an existing application that depends on standard ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ broker protocols and behavior.
column4:
SQS is AWS-native and simpler; Amazon MQ reduces rewriting for broker-compatible applications.
Example: A legacy JMS application moves to managed ActiveMQ on Amazon MQ.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::comparison topic::Application_integration topic::Messaging

column2: How do Amazon MSK and Amazon Kinesis Data Streams differ?
column3: MSK provides managed Apache Kafka compatibility; Kinesis is an AWS-native streaming service.
column4:
Existing Kafka clients and tooling point to MSK; a new AWS-native stream may favor Kinesis.
Example: A company keeps Kafka APIs with MSK instead of rewriting producers.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::comparison topic::Application_integration topic::Streaming

column2: How do AWS AppSync and Amazon API Gateway differ?
column3: AppSync provides managed GraphQL APIs and real-time data features; API Gateway publishes and manages REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs.
column4:
The API style in the question is usually the strongest clue.
Example: A GraphQL mobile backend uses AppSync; a REST Lambda API uses API Gateway.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::comparison topic::APIs

column2: When should a workload use RDS, DynamoDB, or Redshift?
column3: RDS for relational transactions, DynamoDB for serverless key-value/document access at scale, and Redshift for analytical warehousing.
column4:
These services optimize different data models and access patterns.
Example: Orders with SQL relationships use RDS; sessions use DynamoDB; company-wide BI uses Redshift.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-15 chat::2026-09-15_-_Chat_12_—_Analytics_&_Application_Integration type::comparison topic::Databases

column2: How do AWS Local Zones and AWS Wavelength Zones differ?
column3: Local Zones place AWS infrastructure near a metro area; Wavelength Zones place AWS services inside telecom networks for low-latency 5G applications.
column4:
Both extend AWS closer to users, but Wavelength is specifically tied to carrier networks.
Example: Interactive media in a city may use a Local Zone; a 5G connected-vehicle app may use Wavelength.

column3: CloudWatch monitors live operational data and raises alarms; Trusted Advisor periodically recommends best-practice improvements.

column3: CloudWatch: how is it behaving? CloudTrail: who called the API? Config: what was configured and was it compliant?

The three services complement each other during operations and investigation.

column3: AWS Pricing Calculator.

column3: Architecture Center teaches designs and best practices; Marketplace lets customers obtain third-party software, data, and services.

Architecture Center is guidance, while Marketplace is a procurement and deployment catalog.

column2: When should a company choose AWS CloudHSM instead of AWS KMS?
column3: Choose CloudHSM when dedicated single-tenant HSMs and direct control of HSM users, keys, and cryptographic operations are required. Choose KMS for the usual managed encryption-key experience integrated with AWS services.
column4:
Both services protect keys with HSMs. The exam-level difference is operational control and tenancy, not the outdated shortcut that KMS is only “FIPS Level 2.”
Example: A bank with a mandate for dedicated HSM appliances may use CloudHSM; an S3 encryption key normally fits KMS.

column2: How is responsibility divided for an AWS CloudHSM cluster?
column3: AWS operates the physical service and underlying infrastructure; the customer administers HSM users, keys, policies, and cryptographic use.
column4:
CloudHSM gives the customer more control and therefore more operational responsibility than KMS.
Example: AWS replaces failed hardware, while the customer controls who can use a key inside the HSM.
column5: CLF-C02 Security and Compliance day::2026-09-18 chat::2026-09-18_-_Chat_14_—_Security,_Messaging_&_Load_Balancing type::recall topic::Encryption topic::Shared_responsibility

column2: What is the primary purpose of AWS Security Hub?

column4:

column3: AWS Security Hub.

Security Hub consumes and normalizes findings from those services so the team can prioritize remediation centrally.

column2: What does AWS Audit Manager automate?

column3: It is the self-service place to download AWS compliance reports and manage selected agreements.

column2: A security team must apply the same AWS WAF policy across many accounts in AWS Organizations. Which service fits?

Firewall Manager centrally deploys and manages protection policies across accounts and resources.

column3: AWS Config tracks AWS resource configurations and compliance; AWS AppConfig safely deploys application settings and feature flags at runtime.

column2: What does Amazon Inspector scan for?

column2: How do Amazon Inspector and Amazon GuardDuty differ?
column3: Inspector finds vulnerabilities in supported workloads and images; GuardDuty detects suspicious or malicious activity from security signals.

column2: How do Inspector, GuardDuty, Macie, Security Hub, and Trusted Advisor complement one another?

column2: A web application must route /images and /api to different target groups. Which load balancer fits?

column2: A workload needs very high-performance TCP or UDP load balancing and static IP addresses per Availability Zone. Which option fits?

column4:

Example: A real-time game sends UDP traffic through an NLB.
column5: CLF-C02 Cloud Technology and Services day::2026-09-18 chat::2026-09-18_-_Chat_14_—_Security,_Messaging_&_Load_Balancing type::scenario topic::Load_balancing topic::Networking

column2: A company must scale a fleet of third-party firewalls that inspect VPC traffic. Which load balancer fits?
column3: A Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB).
column4:

Example: Traffic passes through a scalable fleet of inspection appliances before reaching workloads.

column2: How do ALB, NLB, GWLB, and Classic Load Balancer differ?
